A practical method for summarising long documents with AI: split by section, summarise in layers, keep references, then check the source.

Long documents are where summarising goes wrong. Ask a model to compress a hundred-page report in a single request and you get something that reads smoothly, sounds confident, and has quietly dropped the qualification on page seventy-four that changes what the finding means. The failure is structural rather than careless: one pass has no memory of what it left out.

This guide is a method, not a product recommendation. It works with any model that accepts long input, and it rests on three ideas — work in layers, keep a reference attached to every claim, and check the result against the original before anyone acts on it.

Why single-shot summaries fail

Three failure modes account for most bad summaries, and they tend to arrive together:

  • Detail collapse. Numbers, dates and names disappear first, because they carry the least readable weight and the highest verification cost.
  • Flattening. A cautious claim and a strong claim end up as one sentence of moderate confidence, and the reader cannot tell which was which.
  • Confident blending. Two sources that disagree are merged into a single smooth statement that neither of them made.

All three come from the same place: a model optimising for readable compression when what you need is faithful compression. The fix is procedural — change how you ask, not which tool you ask.

Step 1: Prepare the document

Before anything reaches a model, prepare the file. Strip repeating headers, footers, page numbers and the parts of the reference list you do not need, because they consume attention and add noise. Keep the headings: section titles are the skeleton of any summary, and a document pasted in without them becomes a wall of undifferentiated text.

Then split by section rather than by character count. Sections are the natural unit of meaning, so each chunk arrives with its own argument intact. For a report, treat each chapter as a chunk. For a contract, treat each article or clause group as one. Arbitrary slices cut sentences in half and hand the model fragments it will happily interpret.

Finally, write one line about purpose: who will read the summary, and what they will do with it. A summary for a decision-maker and a summary for an archive are different documents, and no model can guess which one you need.

Step 2: Summarise in layers

Summarise in two layers, then assemble. The first layer produces a short summary per section — a paragraph at most, written as statements rather than notes. The second layer asks for an overview built only from those section summaries, so the top-level summary inherits the document's structure instead of re-reading everything through one window.

LayerQuestion it answersOutput
Section passWhat does this part say?One paragraph per section
Overview passWhat is the document's argument?One page, built from section summaries
Detail passWhat exactly does it say about X?Quotes with locations

What it means for you: you keep a level of detail you can audit. When someone challenges a line in your overview, you descend to the section summary and then to the quote, instead of re-running the whole document and getting a different answer this time.

Step 3: Keep a reference trail

Ask for a location with every claim: a page number, a section heading, or the opening words of the sentence it came from. If the model cannot give one, ask it to quote the passage directly. Quoted text can be searched in the original file; a paraphrase cannot, and an unlocated claim forces you to re-read the document to check it.

Store the quote next to the claim rather than in a separate list. Detached quotes rot — within a week nobody remembers which point they were supposed to support, and the citation becomes decoration.

What it means for you: your summary becomes checkable in seconds rather than hours. That single property is the difference between a document you can circulate and one you quietly hesitate to send because you know how much of it you have not verified.

Step 4: Check the summary against the source

Verification does not require reading the whole document again. Pick three or four sections at random, ask what each one said, and compare against the original yourself. Then check every number, name and negation directly — those are the items most often distorted, and a single dropped word can invert a clause entirely.

Run the check first on a document you already know well, and you will see what this particular model tends to lose. The pattern is usually consistent — footnotes, scope conditions, dates — and it tells you exactly what to instruct for on the next document you have not read.

Finally, ask one question of both the document and the summary: what would have to be true for this conclusion to be wrong? If the summary has dropped the conditions that qualify the finding, you hold a summary of the conclusion with none of its limits, and that is the version people repeat in meetings.

The same extraction and verification routine underpins our longer AI research workflow, and the checks here are a lighter version of the fact-checking pass we recommend before anything is published. For the mechanics of handling very large inputs across two assistants, our ChatGPT vs Claude comparison explains where each one is stronger.

Common mistakes, and a checklist

Five shortcuts account for most of the summaries people end up distrusting:

  1. Compressing in one request. It is faster, and it produces exactly the smooth, untraceable document described at the start of this guide.
  2. Pasting the document without headings. Structure in, structure out; a flat wall of text invites a flat summary.
  3. Accepting a summary that carries no locations. An unlocated claim cannot be checked, and unchecked claims accumulate until nobody knows which lines are load-bearing.
  4. Testing whether it sounds right. Readability is not accuracy — a fluent summary is precisely what a distorted one looks like.
  5. Summarising for nobody in particular. Without a reader and a decision, you cannot tell an omission from a relief.

Run this before you send anything on: sections split on natural boundaries, at least two layers, a location attached to every claim you intend to keep, numbers and negations spot-checked, and the qualifying conditions still present. It adds minutes. It removes the specific embarrassment of a colleague finding the line your summary quietly changed.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best way to summarise a long document?

Split it by section, summarise each section in one pass, then ask for a second-pass overview built only from those section summaries. Require a location or a quote for every claim you intend to keep. The layered approach takes slightly longer than a single request and produces a summary you can defend to a colleague.

Can AI summarize PDFs accurately?

Usually, if the file contains selectable text and is not full of scans, tables or unusual layouts. Layout-heavy documents lose figures and footnotes during conversion, and that is where summaries go wrong. For scanned or complex files, extract the text first, confirm nothing was dropped, and compare the opening and closing sections against the original.

How do I check an AI summary for accuracy?

Pick several sections at random, ask what each one said, and compare against the original yourself. Check every number, name and negation directly, since those are the items most often distorted. Then ask what would change the document's main conclusion, and confirm the summary did not quietly drop the conditions that qualify it.
